video.title: The Most Useful AI Skill You Can Learn Today

summary: Chris Koerner interviews a Canadian developer/YouTuber (Mike, X handle 'Rasmiki') about how non-technical people can use AI automation and vibe-coding tools. He urges viewers to build at least one automation, shares his AI pizza-ordering agent, and explains n8n webhooks for packaging automations into web apps. The key advice is to solve problems from your own industry (outside the tech bubble), use UX/design taste as a moat, pick LLMs by task (Claude for code, OpenAI for consumer chat, Gemini for cost), and keep learning tools. Business ideas are mostly illustrative and unvalidated.

ideas.name: Industry-specific AI app built by an insider (e.g. pharmacy software)
ideas.one_liner: Domain insiders use AI/vibe-coding tools to build software for the boring, compliance-heavy pain points of their own industry.
ideas.business_model: Software subscription or sales to businesses in a niche industry (not specified in detail).
ideas.customer: Professionals and businesses in a specific industry, e.g. pharmacies.
ideas.problem: Annoying billing, medication-registration software and compliance burdens that tech-bubble builders find boring and ignore.
ideas.offer: A tailored app or wrapper solving a specific workflow pain point in the builder's own industry.

acquisition_channels.details: Distribute wrappers to friends and co-workers in the industry to test and gather feedback, then iterate.

quote.text: I'm gonna take the top three and build rappers from these three and distribute them to my friends and co-workers just to test and play around with
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Built with AI/vibe-coding tools by the industry insider; hosted software.

acquisition.how: Outreach to personal network is human; later marketing in niche could use content/SEO with tooling.

onboarding.how: Self-serve SaaS onboarding can be largely automated.

delivery.how: Software product runs itself once built; agents can maintain it with occasional human review.

support.how: AI support with human escalation for compliance questions.

uk_applicability.notes: Approach is general; UK pharmacy or other regulated sectors have their own compliance (e.g. NHS, GDPR) requiring adaptation.

risks: Regulated industries (pharmacy) carry compliance and data-protection obligations
Builder needs real domain knowledge and distribution
No validation or revenue evidence given

ideas.name: AI-first bookkeeping app
ideas.one_liner: A bookkeeping/receipt app built AI-first, ideally by an accountant or bookkeeper who knows the pain points.
ideas.customer: Individuals and small businesses handling tax season and receipts.
ideas.problem: Receipt tracking is annoying and existing apps (QuickBooks, Xero) miscategorise transactions, e.g. rent as business.
ideas.offer: AI-first bookkeeping that categorises transactions and receipts correctly.

acquisition.how: Inbound SEO/content and app-store listings can be agent-driven.

onboarding.how: Self-serve connection of bank feeds and receipt uploads.

delivery.how: AI categorisation runs automatically; occasional human review of errors.

support.how: AI support with human handling of tax-related edge cases.

uk_applicability.notes: UK needs HMRC Making Tax Digital compatibility and UK VAT/tax categories; crowded with Xero, FreeAgent, QuickBooks.

risks: Accuracy errors in tax contexts carry liability

quotes.text: I really wanted to build an AI bookkeeping app. Tax season is hell. Keeping up with receipts is annoying.
quotes.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

ideas.name: Church / charity payment solution
ideas.one_liner: Cheaper donation-payment software for churches and charities, built by an insider who knew the problem.
ideas.business_model: Software with fairer fees than competitors (payment processing / subscription).
ideas.problem: Existing charity payment software is terrible and charges very high percentages; Stripe alone needs a website to be built.
ideas.offer: A payment solution priced more fairly than competitors.
ideas.delivery: Software built by the speaker for his own church; not commercialised.

acquisition.how: Church/charity buyers often need trust and relationships.

onboarding.how: Payment onboarding and KYC partly automatable.

delivery.how: Payment software runs unattended with occasional approvals.

billing.how: Fees taken automatically via payment processor.

support.how: AI first-line support, human for payment disputes.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has Gift Aid, Charity Commission rules and FCA/payment regulations; competitors like GoCardless, Stripe, Give.Br exist.

quotes.text: I was like, "Huh, I'm going to build a payment solution for my church." And I did that.

ideas.name: AI pizza-ordering agent (Domino's)
ideas.one_liner: Chatbot web app with an AI agent that converses with the user and places a Domino's order via an unofficial API.
ideas.problem: Convenience of ordering pizza through chat.
ideas.offer: Chat interface with agent that gathers order details, stores them in a DB, then calls the Domino's API and pays.
ideas.delivery: Software agent calling an unofficial Domino's API.

billing.how: Payment handled via insecure unofficial API.

uk_applicability.notes: Depends on an unofficial Domino's Canada API; UK would need a different integration and it is not a viable business.

ideas.name: Packaged n8n automation as web app (webhooks + vibe coding)
ideas.one_liner: Wrap an n8n automation behind a simple web front-end using webhooks, e.g. a shoe price-drop alert service.
ideas.business_model: Sell an easy interface to an automation (e.g. subscription); not specified.
ideas.customer: Consumers or users who want simple tools (e.g. shoe price alerts).
ideas.problem: Automations are hard for non-technical users to use; they need a simple interface.
ideas.offer: A web app where the user enters their email, and the automation scrapes for a shoe price and notifies them when it drops.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK; marketing emails to subscribers need consent under PECR/GDPR and scraping must respect site terms.

tactics.name: Mine industry pain points with ChatGPT deep research
steps: Tell ChatGPT your profession and ask for common pain points in that industry
Use deep research to scan Reddit, message boards and social media for gripes and complaints
Take the 7 most relevant of the 20 returned and ask for 20 more like them
Repeat until you have 30-50 problems that ring true
Pick the top three, build wrappers, share with friends and co-workers, and iterate on feedback

quote.text: Pretty soon, you'll have 30 to 50 problems, and all of them will ring true to you as someone in the industry.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Package an n8n automation as a product via webhooks
steps: Build the automation in n8n
Search 'n8n webhooks' and read the first doc
Create a webhook trigger so a web app can send user input (e.g. email) to the workflow
Use a vibe-coding tool (e.g. Tempo) to build the front end
Expect several attempts and debugging

quote.text: I can connect this automation with a web app and that's when it becomes interesting.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

tactics.name: Recreate a site's design with screenshot-to-AI workflow
steps: Screenshot the target site
Feed the screenshot to a vibe-coding tool and ask it to copy the design
Expect roughly 40% fidelity
Go section by section telling the model what is off (button roundness, gradients, spacing)
Iterate until pixel-close

quote.text: The way you get the 40% to 100 is by going through every section of the site that doesn't look pixel perfect and telling it.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

tactics.name: Debug by screenshotting errors into ChatGPT
steps: Screenshot each error or stuck point
Ask ChatGPT what happened and how to learn from it
Retry, or return the next day

quote.text: I will literally either screenshot whatever error I've experienced or where I've got stuck at and let's chat GBT what happened and how do I learn from this?
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

tactics.name: Build design taste
steps: Collect sites and apps you wish you had built
Study frameworks and component libraries such as Magic UI
Analyse what makes Apple's style work: fonts, spacing, bento grid
Use that taste to guide AI tools

warnings.warning: The Domino's agent was never published because it relied on an unofficial API with no secure payment handling.

quote.text: there's no really secure way to handle payment. So, it's a little sus, which is why I only built it for myself.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

warnings.warning: Don't start in the crowded tech bubble as a beginner; competition is intense.

quote.text: This tech bubble we're in is not the best place to start, especially if you're a beginner.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

warnings.warning: Don't prompt a vibe-coding tool with no plan or understanding; expect failures, especially with databases and back ends.

quote.text: most people don't even know the different types of databases and are frustrated when after one prompt
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

warnings.warning: Model recommendations go stale quickly; Claude 3.7 was previously dropped as a waste of money before Claude 4 changed his mind.

lessons.lesson: Build at least one small automation for a task you do regularly; learning by doing beats watching.

quote.text: build at least one after this episode, at least one automation that does something that you do on a regular basis
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

lessons.lesson: The best opportunities are in industries you already know, where you understand customers' problems and how to reach them.

quote.text: the best problems to solve are your own. Number two, the best problems are to solve are the ones that you're in that industry
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

lessons.lesson: Boring, compliance-heavy industry problems are where money is because tech-bubble builders ignore them.

quote.text: It sounds boring, but that's where the money is.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

lessons.lesson: Building is only part one; marketing is a separate challenge, easier if you are inside the industry.
UX and design taste can be a moat; customers will pay more for polished experiences.

quote.text: I think UX becomes a moat.
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

lessons.lesson: Choose LLMs per task: Claude for code/agentic, OpenAI for consumer chat and personality, Gemini for cost; beginners should default to OpenAI. Cost matters little at the prototyping stage.
Stay flexible and switch tools when better models launch; knowledge from failed experiments still compounds.

quote.text: Part of the game is being able to know, okay, what's out, what's popping, which one's doing great, and then being able to move over
quote.speaker: Mike (Rasmiki)

lessons.lesson: Non-technical founders should learn base technical concepts (front end, back end, auth, database) and keep developer friends.
MCP standardises LLM access to third-party services, reducing custom API integration work.
Beginners may build a landing page first for momentum, but experienced builders should build the product first and treat design separately.

evidence_quality.rationale: Mostly general advice and illustrative ideas; the guest's only concrete builds (pizza agent, church payments) are unmonetised, and no first-hand revenue figures are given. Third-party numbers are hearsay.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host promotes TK Owners ($99/month community) and his newsletter; guest uses and mentions Tempo (a vibe-coding tool) and admits bias.
